subtype: Knowing when to involve an adult [Regulating]
passage: When I was in Class Ten, Jeevan, your grandmother's friend Meena told me something at the school bus stop, and her voice was flat. She said she had been saying to herself that she did not want to be here anymore. She made me promise not to tell anyone. I said yes, because I did not know what else to say. That night I could not eat. I knew a promise to a friend mattered, but I also knew this was too big for me. In the morning I told our class teacher, Mrs Rao, with shaking hands. Meena was angry for a week. Later she hugged me and said, "Thank you for not leaving me alone with it."

qa.q: Where did Meena tell the narrator her secret?
qa.a: She told it at the school bus stop.

qa.q: What was the narrator feeling the night after promising?
qa.a: The narrator was frightened and troubled, too upset to eat, and knew the promise mattered but also saw the problem was too big to hold alone.

qa.q: What should a teenager do if a friend shares something this serious?
qa.a: Tell a trusted adult, such as a teacher or parent, soon, even if the friend asked for secrecy, and stay kind to the friend afterwards.

qa.q: How might Meena have felt when she found out the teacher knew?
qa.a: She may have felt betrayed and exposed for a while, and later relieved and cared for.

grounding: A teen recognises a worry as too big to hold and tells a trusted adult despite a promise of secrecy.

passage: The power cut hit just as the evening rain got heavy. Vaibhav and Payal were sheltering at the bus stop, his phone at four percent. Payal was staring at the puddles. "Promise you won't tell anyone," she said. "My uncle's messages make me feel unsafe. He tells me not to say anything." Vaibhav's throat tightened. "Payal, I can't promise that. Someone has to know so you're safe." She cried a little. He typed a quick message to his mother, "I need to bring a friend home, it's about safety," and the phone died. They walked together through the rain, and the next morning he sat beside her in the counsellor's office and did not leave until she asked him to.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav's phone battery at the bus stop?
qa.a: His phone was at four percent.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav refuse to promise Payal that he would stay quiet?
qa.a: He felt that her safety mattered more than the secret, so a promise not to tell could have left her alone with the danger. His tightened throat shows he cared and was afraid for her.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do that was helpful under pressure?
qa.a: He sent a message to his mother, stayed with Payal and went with her to the counsellor the next morning.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt when he would not promise silence?
qa.a: She may have felt afraid or let down at first, and still glad that someone took it seriously.

grounding: A teenager tells a trusted adult about a safety worry even though a friend asked for secrecy.

The colony park was nearly empty at seven, the lamps just coming on. Harsha sat on the swing without swinging.
"Madhav, promise you won't tell anyone. Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me."
Madhav's stomach turned cold. He didn't laugh it off or change the subject.
"Thank you for telling me," he said. "I care about you too much to keep this one. Come with me to my mother now. I'll stay with you the whole time."
Harsha shook her head, then slowly stood up.
Madhav's mother was on the balcony. She came down at once, sat with Harsha on the bench, and listened without rushing her. She said, "You did the right thing. None of this is your fault." Then, with Harsha beside her, she phoned Harsha's parents, who came straight over. Before the night ended, they had spoken to a counsellor on a helpline together.

qa.q: Where was Harsha sitting when she spoke to Madhav?
qa.a: Harsha sat on the swing in the colony park without swinging.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when Harsha said everyone would be better off without her?
qa.a: Madhav felt frightened, his stomach turning cold, but his care for Harsha was stronger than the promise.

qa.q: Which of Madhav's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Refusing to keep the secret, staying with Harsha and taking her straight to his mother meant a trusted adult acted that same evening.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt as Madhav's mother listened and called her parents?
qa.a: She may have felt scared and exposed at first, but also relieved not to carry the feeling alone any more.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager recognising self-harm talk as too big to hold alone and telling a trusted adult immediately despite a request for secrecy.

"Vidya, why are you wearing a sweater? It's so hot."
"Just cold."
"Tenzin knows you. Tenzin's not stupid."
Vidya looked at the corridor floor. "If I tell you, you have to swear not to say it to anyone."
"Tell me first."
"My uncle. When he drinks. He grabs my arm. Last night it was worse."
Tenzin took a breath. "Thank you for telling me. I can't swear to keep that one. It's too big, and it isn't your fault."
"You'll make it worse."
"I'll come with you. Right now. Mrs Lobo's room is just there."
Mrs Lobo, the counsellor, looked up as they came in. She listened to Vidya without interrupting, said clearly it was not her fault, and told her she would not be sent home alone today. Then she called the school's safeguarding lead into the room while Tenzin waited outside.

qa.q: Where was Mrs Lobo's room?
qa.a: Mrs Lobo's room was just there, off the corridor.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when she asked Tenzin to swear secrecy?
qa.a: Vidya was scared and ashamed, worried that telling would make things worse at home.

qa.q: Which of Tenzin's choices helped Vidya most?
qa.a: Tenzin thanked Vidya, refused to promise secrecy about harm, said it wasn't her fault, and walked her straight to the counsellor.

qa.q: How did Mrs Lobo respond, and what did it show Vidya?
qa.a: She listened, said it wasn't Vidya's fault, promised she wouldn't be sent home alone, and brought in the safeguarding lead, showing Vidya that telling led to protection.

grounding: The dialogue shows a teenager recognising abuse as too big to keep secret and taking a friend to a trusted adult who acts the same day.

passage:
I still think about the evening Sabina showed me her phone on the bus home. It was full of messages from her ex. "I know where you live." "I'll wait outside your gate." She laughed it off. "He's just angry. Don't tell anyone, Thomas, it'll blow over."
I nodded. But at home I couldn't eat. I kept picturing him at her gate.
So I told my mum over dinner. She put down her spoon and said, "You were right to tell me." She called Sabina's mother that same evening, and then drove me over so Sabina wasn't alone when her parents saw the messages. Her parents took screenshots and told the school the next morning.
Sabina was cold with me for a few days. Then one afternoon she said, "I was more scared than I said." I think that's the moment I understood care sometimes means breaking a promise.

qa.q: What did one of the ex's messages say?
qa.a: One said, "I know where you live."

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling at home after the bus ride?
qa.a: Thomas felt frightened for Sabina and too anxious to eat, torn between the promise and the picture of the ex waiting at her gate.

qa.q: Which choice of Thomas's worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling Mum that same evening worked, because she called Sabina's mother and went over so the adults could protect Sabina right away.

qa.q: How might Sabina have seen Thomas's choice at first compared with later?
qa.a: At first she felt betrayed and was cold with Thomas, but later she admitted she was more scared than she said, suggesting she saw it as care.

grounding: The reflective account shows a teenager recognising threats as too big to keep secret and telling a trusted adult despite a friend's request.

Counsellor's note, Thursday
At 12:50 Dhruv knocked and stood in the doorway for a long moment before sitting. He kept twisting his watch strap. He said Jomon had messaged him last night: "don't tell anyone, but sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me." Dhruv said he had promised to keep it secret and felt like a traitor for coming. I told him he had done exactly the right thing, that this was too big for one friend to hold, and that he was not in trouble, and neither was Jomon. I asked him to wait in my room while I fetched Jomon from the lab myself. I spoke with Jomon until 2:30; his mother came to school at 3 and we made a safety plan together. Before Dhruv left, I said he could check in with me tomorrow. He asked, "Will Jomon hate me?" I said Jomon might be upset for a while, and that caring sometimes feels like that.

qa.q: What time did Dhruv knock?
qa.a: Dhruv knocked at 12:50.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling as he twisted his watch strap?
qa.a: Dhruv felt anxious and guilty, torn between the promise and fear for Jomon; the long pause in the doorway also suggests he feared being blamed.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do straight away that helped?
qa.a: The counsellor told Dhruv he had done the right thing, fetched Jomon at once, talked with Jomon until 2:30, and brought in Jomon's mother that afternoon to make a safety plan.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel about Dhruv telling?
qa.a: Jomon might feel upset or betrayed at first, but being met straight away by the counsellor and a parent may also bring relief at not carrying it alone.

grounding: It shows a teenager recognising that a friend's hopeless message is too big to hold alone and telling a trusted adult despite being asked for secrecy.
